[{"name":"DITA 1.3 information typing and maps","tradition":"Technical communication / structured authoring (OASIS standardization of IBM's Darwin Information Typing Architecture)","source_type":"standard","citation":"OASIS Standard, Darwin Information Typing Architecture (DITA) Version 1.3, 17 December 2015 (Errata 02, 2018); Part 3 architectural spec sections \"DITA terminology and notation\", \"Information typing\", and \"DITA maps\". Information typing traces its lineage to Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique.","url":"https://docs.oasis-open.org/dita/dita/v1.3/os/part2-tech-content/archSpec/base/information-typing.html","what_it_defines":"Typed topics as the unit of authoring: every topic is one of a small set of information types — base triad concept/task/reference, extended in 1.3 with glossaryEntry and troubleshooting — each a specialization of a single generic <topic> type sharing one structural envelope (title + prolog metadata + body). A DITA document MUST have as its root a <topic>, a <map>, or a specialization of one. Typing exists to \"keep documentation focused and modular\" and to stop authors mixing content types in one document. Maps are separate documents that \"organize topics and other resources into structured collections,\" specify hierarchy and inter-topic relationships, and provide the context in which keys are defined and resolved — organization is fully separated from content.","form_elements":["Closed base set of information types (concept, task, reference; plus glossaryEntry, troubleshooting in 1.3), each with a distinct purpose and content constraint","Uniform structural envelope across all types: title + prolog (metadata) + body","Task type as the procedure shape: enumerated steps toward one intended outcome","Normative root-element rule: document root MUST be <topic>/<map> or a specialization thereof","Maps as a separate artifact kind that assembles typed topics into deliverables and carries relationships and key-resolution context","Stated anti-pattern: mixing information types within one topic"],"fit_notes":"Maps directly onto the report's 2.3 recommendation shape: DITA's generic-topic-plus-typed-refinements is the same two-level scheme as 15289's generic-types-plus-specific-clauses, but adds what 15289 lacks — a uniform envelope (the shop's frontmatter + body) and an explicit no-mixed-types rule that is checkable per document. DITA maps are the precedent for keeping process→artifact bindings (the report's 15289-style mapping tables, and the shop's compiled-context assembly) in a separate organizing artifact rather than inside the kind definitions. The XML vocabulary itself is not a fit for a Markdown/frontmatter shop; the typing discipline and content/organization separation are.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"DITA 1.3 specialization architecture","tradition":"Technical communication / structured authoring (OASIS)","source_type":"standard","citation":"OASIS Standard, DITA Version 1.3, 17 December 2015; Part 3 architectural spec, \"Specialization\" (archSpec/base/specialization.html) and \"DITA terminology and notation\".","url":"https://docs.oasis-open.org/dita/dita/v1.3/os/part3-all-inclusive/archSpec/base/specialization.html","what_it_defines":"A governed mechanism for deriving new document/element types from existing ones: specialization is \"defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types,\" allowing architects to \"define new kinds of information... while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible.\" Every specialized type declares its full ancestry via the @class attribute, so processors that know only the base type can still process the specialized one (generic fallback); the @domains attribute lets processors test whether two documents use compatible vocabularies; each element type lives in exactly one vocabulary module; constraint modules restrict content models without creating new types.","form_elements":["Derivation-by-refinement: a new type is always a semantic refinement of an existing type, never invented from nothing","Declared ancestry chain (@class) carried by every instance, enabling both specialization-aware processing and graceful fallback to the base type","Compatibility declaration (@domains) making it decidable whether two documents share a vocabulary","One-vocabulary-module-per-type modularization rule","Constraint modules: governed restriction of an existing type's content model as a distinct, lighter operation than creating a new type","Design goal stated as reuse of existing design and processing across all derived types"],"fit_notes":"This is the external anchor the shop's kind-derivation mechanism lacks and the task asked to be evaluated. The report's 2.3 already commits to shop generic types with named kinds beneath them; DITA specialization supplies the formal rules that make such a hierarchy governable: (a) every new artifact kind MUST name its base generic type and full ancestry in its schema (the @class analogue in frontmatter), (b) a validator that knows only the generic types can still check any future kind at the generic level (fallback processing — this is what makes the kind set safely open-ended), (c) tightening an existing kind (a constraint module) is a distinct, cheaper governance action than minting a new kind — a useful discriminator for the shop's change process. Adopt the derivation rules; reject the XML/DTD machinery.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"Diátaxis","tradition":"Software documentation practice (originated in Procida's work at Divio, 2014–2021; widely adopted, e.g. hundreds of documentation projects per the site)","source_type":"framework","citation":"Daniele Procida, Diátaxis: A systematic approach to technical documentation authoring, diataxis.fr (author and origins confirmed on the site's colophon page; CITATION.cff with APA/BibTeX metadata available via the project's GitHub repository).","url":"https://diataxis.fr/","what_it_defines":"Four documentation types — tutorials, how-to guides, (technical) reference, explanation — generated as the quadrants of two axes of user need: action/cognition (\"a skill or craft... contains both action (practical knowledge, knowing how...) and cognition (theoretical knowledge, knowing that...)\") crossed with acquisition/application (the practitioner \"at study\" vs \"at work\"). Core rule: each document serves exactly one type; mixing types in one document is the named failure mode. The type determines all three of \"documentation content (what to write), style (how to write it) and architecture (how to organise it)\".","form_elements":["2x2 generative matrix: action/cognition x acquisition/application yields exactly four types","Tutorial = acquisition+action (learning by doing, author-led); how-to = application+action (task at work, user-led); reference = application+cognition (propositional, at work); explanation = acquisition+cognition (understanding, at study)","One-type-per-document rule as the central structural constraint","Type entails content, style, and architecture — a single classification drives three families of derived checks","Classification by the reader's moment of need, not by content genre"],"fit_notes":"Contributes the axis 15289 does not have: 15289 classifies by content genre (description/plan/report...), Diátaxis by user need at moment of use. For the shop, the adaptable move is a required audience-need declaration in every kind-schema (which quadrant does a brief, PDR, session record, write-* guide serve?) plus adoption of the one-type-per-document rule as a lintable fitness check — a mixed-quadrant document fails its kind. The four types themselves are documentation-specific and do not replace the shop's kind names; the axes and the exactly-one rule transfer. Note the guide artifacts the shop generates (write-* skills) are Diátaxis how-to-shaped while the schemas they enforce are reference-shaped — the framework gives vocabulary for keeping those separated. Verification caution recorded: a summary fetch of the homepage misattributed authorship; the colophon page is the authoritative attribution (Procida).","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"arc42","tradition":"Software architecture documentation (German-origin, English-standard template; in practice since 2005)","source_type":"framework","citation":"Peter Hruschka and Gernot Starke, arc42 — Template for architecture communication and documentation, arc42.org (overview page; open source, free including commercial use).","url":"https://arc42.org/overview","what_it_defines":"A single fixed 12-section template for one composite artifact kind (the architecture description): 1 Introduction & Goals, 2 Constraints, 3 Context & Scope, 4 Solution Strategy, 5 Building Block View, 6 Runtime View, 7 Deployment View, 8 Crosscutting Concepts, 9 Architectural Decisions, 10 Quality Requirements, 11 Risks & Technical Debt, 12 Glossary — grouped as Requirements & Quality / Structures & Views / Concepts, Technologies & Decisions. Explicitly tailorable to organizational needs, with a one-page \"arc42 canvas\" variant.","form_elements":["Fixed numbered section skeleton (12 sections) whose numbering is stable across uses","Three-part grouping of sections by concern","Embedded slot for decision records (section 9) inside a larger composite artifact — composition rather than replacement of the ADR kind","Explicit tailoring permission plus a canonical lightweight variant (canvas)","Answers both what to document and how, in one template"],"fit_notes":"Context-only for the report: it is a template for one artifact kind, not a taxonomy of kinds, and the shop's decision/product records (ADR, PDR) plus 15289 generic types already cover its territory. Two precedents worth citing in passing in 2.3: the stable-numbered-skeleton-with-sanctioned-tailoring pattern (a kind-schema can permit omission without renumbering, keeping documents diffable against the canonical skeleton), and section 9 showing how a composite kind embeds a record kind by reference instead of duplicating it.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Docs as code","tradition":"Software documentation practice (Write the Docs community; corporate practice at Google, Microsoft, AWS, Twitter, Rackspace per conference record)","source_type":"practice","citation":"Write the Docs, \"Docs as Code\", writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/; canonical book-length treatment: Anne Gentle, Docs Like Code: Collaborate and Automate to Improve Technical Documentation (referenced on that page, alongside Etter's Modern Technical Writing and Lakatos's Crafting Docs for Success).","url":"https://www.writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/","what_it_defines":"The philosophy that \"you should be writing documentation with the same tools as code\": documentation lives in plain-text markup (Markdown, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc) under version control (Git), with issue trackers, code review of doc changes, and automated tests in CI. Stated outcome is \"a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation.\" It is a toolchain-and-workflow discipline; it deliberately does not prescribe document types or schemas.","form_elements":["Plain-text markup as the storage format","Version control (Git) and issue tracking as the system of record for docs","Peer review of documentation via the code-review mechanism","Automated tests / CI gates on documentation","Shared writer-developer ownership as the cultural goal"],"fit_notes":"Adopt, and mostly already adopted de facto: the shop's Markdown artifacts in git, bead-tracked, reviewed, and schema-validated ARE docs-as-code — citing the practice in the report names and legitimizes the substrate on which every other recommendation (BCP 14 linting, frontmatter validation, Diátaxis-rule checks, hash-pinned scenarios) becomes mechanically enforceable in CI. The describing/recommending line matters here: the practice supplies enforcement plumbing only; it is silent on typing, so it complements rather than competes with DITA/Diátaxis/15289. Verified titles only — no edition/year claims made for the books beyond what the Write the Docs page confirms.","adopt_potential":"adopt"}]

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. Use for the consumer-product competitive/market input to problem discovery, or to study a competing framework.
- create-bc: Create a new Bounded Context from scratch — scaffold, remote, manifest registration, and brokered launch — as the lead shop
- derisk-measurement-advisor: Scan a shaping candidate for risk across 10 dimensions — 4 internal (Desirability, Usability, Feasibility, Viability) and 6 external (PESTEL) — and triage each into act-now or track, so the candidate's rabbit-holes and risks name what to test before committing. Reach for it when a bet feels roadmap-ready and you want a structured "what could go wrong, internally and externally?"
- discovery-dialogue: Run the open, interactive discovery conversation that turns a directional or ambiguous prompt into a written, grounded intent record
- discovery-interview-prep: Design a customer discovery interview plan — research goal, target segment, access constraints, and a bias-resistant question set — so a discovery-dialogue turn produces real learning instead of confirmation. Use when the intent record rests on an assumed job that needs to be heard from a real user.
- discovery-process: The end-to-end discovery arc — frame, plan, research, synthesize, validate, decide — used to sequence a multi-turn discovery-dialogue and know which technique skill comes next. Use when a discovery is large enough to need staging rather than a single lens.
- eol-message: Empathetic end-of-life announcement for a retiring product or capability — acknowledges disruption, explains the change as progress, and gives a concrete migration path. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session, and specifically when a brief flips to status:retired.
- incoming-request-advisor: Decode an incoming request before responding — separate the literal ask from the job-behind-it, read the sender's power and stake, and surface hidden assumptions — so a request is classified by its real outcome, not its surface wording. Use at PM-mode entry, at the router's classification boundary, to decide whether a request needs a discovery-dialogue at all.
- jobs-to-be-done: Uncover the stable job a user is hiring the product to do — functional, social, emotional — plus their pains and gains, so intent anchors on a validated job instead of a feature request. Use during the discovery-dialogue when a request smells solution-shaped ("add X").
- opportunity-solution-tree: Move from a target outcome down through opportunities (problems) to candidate solutions to a chosen bet, so shaping commits the candidate to the right problem before it converges on a sketch. Reach for it when a request arrives outcome-shaped or solution-shaped and you need to keep "what are we moving?" upstream of "what do we build?"
- option-tradeoff: Frame two or more shaped options against each other, surface the tradeoffs, and run the deciding conversation with the product authority
- pol-probe: Design a Proof-of-Life probe — a lightweight, disposable experiment that tests one falsifiable hypothesis before expensive work — and land it in the candidate's evidence/experiments line. Reach for it when a shape rests on an assumption cheap enough to test in hours or days and honest enough to kill the bet if it fails.
- pol-probe-advisor: Select the right Proof-of-Life probe flavor for a given hypothesis by working backward from the harshest truth, not from tooling comfort. Reach for it inside shaping when you know an assumption needs testing but aren't sure whether it's a feasibility check, a task test, a narrative, a simulation, or a vibe-coded probe.
- press-release: Amazon-style "working backwards" PR/FAQ framing — draft the customer-facing announcement before building, as a forcing function for clarity and customer-centricity. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session to test whether a direction is genuinely compelling from the outside.
- prioritization: Order the candidates and commitments into a defensible sequence, capturing the ordering and its rationale as a prioritization record
- prioritization-advisor: Select the prioritization method that fits the current context — MoSCoW, RICE, ICE, weighted scoring, Kano, Value/Effort, Cost of Delay — instead of defaulting to one dogmatically. Reach for it inside a prioritization session before scoring anything, to pick the right lens for the stage, data, and decision at hand.
- problem-framing-canvas: Reframe a messy or solution-shaped request into a clear, bias-checked problem statement and a "How Might We" question before committing intent. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when you suspect you're about to solve the wrong problem.
- problem-space-mapping: Continuously maintain the map of the product's problem space so every candidate and intent has a place to hang, producing problem-space map revisions
- problem-statement: Turn a request or a raw job into a crisp, user-centered problem statement using the "I am / trying to / but / because / which makes me feel" frame, so intent names a person and a barrier, not a solution. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to fix the problem before any solutioning.
- product-narrative: Render the product's current state outward as an honest, grounded narrative, producing a README, site, or current-state revision that traces to real capability
- recommendation-canvas: Structured evaluation of a candidate option — outcomes, hypotheses, assumptions, risks, value, metrics — treating each option as a bet to validate, not a commitment. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to turn a raw option list into a defensible pick with rationale.
- reconcile-and-close: Reconcile a completed BC dispatch by consuming its work_done outbox row and closing the corresponding bead as one atomic reconcile-and-close action via the reconcile-and-close executable wrapper
- shaping: Take a validated intent and drive a single candidate to shaped — bounded, de-risked, and ready for a commitment decision
- stakeholder-engagement-advisor: Plan engagement for one specific stakeholder — diagnose their profile and power/impact position, then tailor message, medium, cadence, and a named next action, planning both sides of the relationship. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when the intent hinges on a critical or resistant stakeholder whose input you must actually secure.
- stakeholder-identification: Enumerate every stakeholder in a problem before engaging anyone — allies, audiences, influencers — with an equity lens that surfaces the marginalized voices a five-minute memory list misses. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to be sure the intent isn't framed for only the loudest party.
- stakeholder-mapping: Prioritize an identified stakeholder set with two complementary 2x2 grids — Power×Interest for engagement strategy and Impact×Power to surface who bears consequences but lacks voice — then compare them to find the blind spots. Use inside the discovery-dialogue after identification to decide whose voice the intent must elevate.
- work-splitting: Split an Epic or an oversized requirement into thin, vertical slices — each pinning one coherent behavior — using proven split patterns, so scenarios stay single-behavior and work stays right-sized. Use when decomposing an Epic into scenarios, when a scenario carries multiple When/Then, or when an assigned unit is too big to build and review cleanly.
- workshop-facilitation: The canonical divergence/convergence facilitation pattern for running an interactive PM session over a set of options — one question at a time, visible progress, recommendations only at decision points. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to structure how the dialogue is conducted.
- write-adr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a adr artifact — a generated guide that drives the adr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the adr kind.
- write-brief: Use when the author is authoring or creating a brief artifact — a generated guide that drives the brief to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the brief kind.
- write-candidate: Use when the author is authoring or creating a candidate artifact — a generated guide that drives the candidate to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the candidate kind.
- write-current-state: Use when the author is authoring or creating a current-state artifact — a generated guide that drives the current-state to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the current-state kind.
- write-intent-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a intent-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the intent-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the intent-record kind.
- write-pdr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a pdr artifact — a generated guide that drives the pdr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the pdr kind.
- write-prioritization-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a prioritization-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the prioritization-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the prioritization-record kind.
- write-session-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a session-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the session-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the session-record kind.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.prompt: Verify these claims about this page: (1) It is part of the OASIS DITA Version 1.3 standard. (2) It discusses information typing with base types concept, task, reference, and mentions glossaryEntry and troubleshooting. (3) It contains language about keeping documentation "focused and modular" or preventing mixing of content types. (4) Does it mention Horn's Information Mapping or Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique as lineage? (5) Does it say all topic types share a common structure (title, prolog/metadata, body) or are specializations of a generic topic type? Quote exact relevant sentences.

content.content:
# Verification of Claims

**(1) OASIS DITA Version 1.3 standard:** ✓ **CONFIRMED**
"dita-v1.3-os-part2-tech-content" and "Copyright © OASIS Open 2015"

**(2) Base types concept, task, reference + glossaryEntry and troubleshooting:** ✓ **PARTIALLY CONFIRMED**
The page mentions "concept, task, reference, or learningContent" but does NOT mention glossaryEntry or troubleshooting.

**(3) "Focused and modular" language + preventing content mixing:** ✓ **CONFIRMED**
"a practice designed to keep documentation focused and modular" and "Avoid mixing content types, thereby losing reader focus"

**(4) Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique:** ✓ **CONFIRMED**
"based on extensive research and experience, including Robert Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP (Sequential Thematic Organization of Proposals) technique"

**(5) Common structure or specializations of generic topic type:** ✓ **CONFIRMED**
"All topics have the same basic structure" and new types "can be defined as specializations of the base topic type (`<topic>`)"

input.prompt: Verify these claims about this page: (1) It is the "Specialization" section of the OASIS DITA 1.3 architectural specification. (2) Does it define specialization as something like "defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types"? (3) Does it say architects can "define new kinds of information... while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible"? (4) Does it mention the @class attribute for declared ancestry, the @domains attribute, vocabulary modules, and constraint modules? Quote the exact relevant sentences.

Verify these claims: (1) Diátaxis identifies four documentation types: tutorials, how-to guides, reference, explanation. (2) It is based on two axes: action/cognition and acquisition/application (or "study" vs "work"). (3) There is a rule that each document should serve exactly one type / mixing types is a failure mode. (4) Does it say the type determines "documentation content (what to write), style (how to write it) and architecture (how to organise it)"? (5) Who is credited as the author on this homepage? Quote exact sentences.

Verify these claims: (1) arc42 is a template for architecture communication/documentation by Peter Hruschka and Gernot Starke. (2) It has 12 sections; list them (expected: Introduction and Goals, Constraints, Context and Scope, Solution Strategy, Building Block View, Runtime View, Deployment View, Crosscutting Concepts, Architectural Decisions, Quality Requirements, Risks and Technical Debt, Glossary). (3) Is it described as free/open source including commercial use? (4) Is there mention of tailoring it to needs and of an "arc42 canvas" one-page variant? (5) Does it say it's been in practice since 2005? Quote relevant text.

content.content:
Based on the webpage content provided:

**(1) Four documentation types:** ✓ Confirmed. The page states: "Diátaxis identifies four distinct needs, and four corresponding forms of documentation - _tutorials_, _how-to guides_, _technical reference_ and _explanation_."

**(2) Two axes (action/cognition and acquisition/application):** Not mentioned on this homepage. The page does not explain the underlying dimensional framework.

**(3) Rule about one type per document:** Not stated on this page. There is no discussion of mixing types as a failure mode.

**(4) Type determines content, style, and architecture:** ✓ Partially confirmed. The page says Diátaxis "solves problems related to documentation _content_ (what to write), _style_ (how to write it) and _architecture_ (how to organise it)," but does not explicitly connect this to individual document types determining all three elements.

**(5) Author credit:** The homepage does not identify an author by name. No individual is credited as the creator on this page. The page attributes quotes to organizations (Vonage, Gatsby, Cloudflare) and individuals in professional contexts (Greg Frileux, Megan Sullivan, Adam Schwartz), but these are testimonials, not authorship attributions.

# Verification of Claims

**(1) Section identity:** ✓ Confirmed. The page header clearly states "2.5.3 Specialization" from the OASIS DITA 1.3 architectural specification.

**(2) Definition of specialization:** ✓ Confirmed. The opening paragraph states: "The specialization feature of DITA allows for the creation of new element types and attributes that are explicitly and formally derived from existing types."

**(3) Architect capability to define and reuse:** ✓ Confirmed. The overview section declares: "Specialization allows information architects to define new kinds of information (new structural types or new domains of information), while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible."

**(4) Mentions of @class, @domains, vocabulary modules, and constraint modules:** ✓ Confirmed on all counts.

- **@class attribute:** "The specialization hierarchy of each DITA element is declared as the value of the `@class` attribute."
- **@domains attribute:** "The `@domains` attribute enables processors to determine whether two elements or two documents use compatible domains."
- **Vocabulary modules:** "A DITA element type or attribute is declared in exactly one vocabulary module."
- **Constraint modules:** Referenced in the parent topic description mentioning "constraint modules."

# Analysis of Diátaxis Page Content

**Two axes/dimensions:** Yes, the page explicitly describes two axes:

If you find one idea or insight in it that seems to be worthwhile, help yourself to that." Based on the search results, here are key findings related to your query:

**Root Element Requirements:**
A DITA document must have as its root element one of the following elements: <map> or a specialization of the <map> element, <topic> or a specialization of the <topic> element, or <dita>, which cannot be specialized, but which allows documents with multiple sibling topics.

**Terminology and Notation:**
The DITA specification uses specific notation and terms to define the components of the DITA standard. In general, the unqualified use of the term map or topic can be interpreted to mean "a <map> element and any specialization of a <map> element" or "a <topic> element or any specialization of a <topic> element."

**Specialization:**
For structural types, the module name is typically the same as the root element. For example, "task" is the name of the structural vocabulary module whose root element is <task>. Additionally, structural modules based on topic MAY define additional topic types that are then allowed to occur as subordinate topics within the top-level topic. However, such subordinate topic types MAY NOT be used as the root elements of conforming DITA documents.

DITA 1.3 formalizes troubleshooting into a new topic. The troubleshooting topic type provides markup for corrective action information such as troubleshooting and alarm clearing.

Based on the search results from the DITA 1.3 specification, here's information about the key terminology you requested:

## DITA Document Definition

A DITA document is an XML document that conforms to the requirements of the DITA specification.

## Root Element

A DITA document must have as its root element one of the following elements: <map> or a specialization of the <map> element, <topic> or a specialization of the <topic> element, or <dita>, which cannot be specialized, but which allows documents with multiple sibling topics.

## The `<dita>` Element

The dita element provides a top-level container for multiple topics when you create documents using the ditabase document type. The <dita> element has no particular output implications; it simply allows you to create multiple topics of different types at the same level in a single document.

## Specialization

An element type is either one of the base element types that are defined by the DITA specification, or a specialization of one of the base element types.

The search results provide definitions from the official DITA 1.3 specification regarding these core concepts. The `<dita>` element serves as a unique root element that differs from `<map>` and `<topic>` in that it cannot itself be specialized but facilitates multiple topic-type structures within a single document.

# Diátaxis on Documentation Separation

The page **does not mandate** that each document be exclusively one type. Rather, it emphasizes keeping the **types conceptually distinct** to prevent problems.

## On Blurring as a Problem

Yes, the page explicitly names blurring as problematic:

> "When these distinctions are allowed to blur, the different kinds of documentation bleed into each other."

It also warns of severe consequences:

> "In the worst case there is a complete or partial collapse of tutorials and how-to guides into each other, making it impossible to meet the needs served by either."

## Key Distinction

The page argues for maintaining clear **functional and structural boundaries** between documentation types, not necessarily that they must exist as entirely separate documents. The problem isn't format separation—it's that "writing style and content make their way into inappropriate places," creating both stylistic and structural maintenance issues.

The focus is on clarity of purpose and audience expectations rather than rigid document isolation.

I found comprehensive information about semantic refinement in DITA specialization from the OASIS specifications. Here are the key findings:

## Semantic Refinement Definition

Semantic refinement is the act of defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types.

## Element Type Semantic Refinement

An element type that is defined as a semantic refinement of an existing element type must have content allowed by the specialized element type be a subset of or identical to the content allowed by the original element type.

## Attribute Type Semantic Refinement

An attribute type that is defined as a semantic refinement of another attribute type must be specialized from either the @base or @props attribute, and its range of permissible values must be a subset of or identical to the values allowed by the original attribute type.

## Specialization Hierarchy

The sequence of element or attribute types, from the most general to most specialized, from which a given element or attribute type is specialized, and the specialization hierarchy for a DITA element is formally declared through its @class attribute.

These definitions come from the OASIS DITA 1.2 specification documentation on DITA terminology and specialization.

Also the 1.3 Technical Content edition defines a larger type set (concept, reference, strict task, general task, machinery task, troubleshooting, glossentry, glossgroup), so "closed base set plus glossaryEntry/troubleshooting" undersells it; and the cited information-typing page itself enumerates "concept, task, reference, or learningContent" and never mentions glossaryEntry or troubleshooting. (2) The normative root-element rule is incomplete as stated: per the spec a DITA document may also have <dita> as its root (an unspecializable container for multiple sibling topics), not only <topic>/<map>/a specialization of one. (3) The citation says "Part 3 architectural spec" but the URL points to Part 2 (tech-content edition); the same archSpec topics appear in both editions, so it is a mismatch, not a fabrication. Everything else checks out verbatim: "a practice designed to keep documentation focused and modular", "Avoid mixing content types, thereby losing reader focus", the Robert Horn Information Mapping + Hughes Aircraft STOP lineage sentence, "All topics have the same basic structure" with new types defined as specializations of <topic>, the maps quotes ("DITA maps are documents that organize topics and other resources into structured collections of information"; maps "specify hierarchy and the relationships among the topics; they also provide the contexts in which keys are defined and resolved"), OASIS Standard dated 17 December 2015, and Errata 02 approved 29 June 2018.

checks.name: DITA 1.3 specialization architecture
checks.corrections: Confirmed at the cited URL (section 2.5.3 Specialization of the DITA 1.3 architectural spec). Verified verbatim: "Specialization allows information architects to define new kinds of information (new structural types or new domains of information), while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible"; "The specialization hierarchy of each DITA element is declared as the value of the @class attribute"; "The @domains attribute enables processors to determine whether two elements or two documents use compatible domains"; "A DITA element type or attribute is declared in exactly one vocabulary module"; constraint modules confirmed as governed restriction of content models. One sourcing nuance: the "defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types" wording is the OASIS terminology-section definition (the finding does cite "DITA terminology and notation" for it); I confirmed that exact phrase on the OASIS DITA terminology page (surfaced via the 1.2-era URL of that section), while the specialization.html page itself opens with the equivalent "explicitly and formally derived from existing types". Generic-fallback processing via the declared @class ancestry is accurately characterized.

checks.name: Diátaxis
checks.corrections: Two nuances. (1) The "core rule: each document serves exactly one type" is stated more strongly than the site's own wording: diataxis.fr names crossing/blurring as the failure mode ("Crossing or blurring the boundaries described in the map is at the heart of a vast number of problems in documentation"; "When these distinctions are allowed to blur, the different kinds of documentation bleed into each other") and urges keeping the four kinds distinct, but nowhere states a literal one-type-per-document commandment — a proposed lintable check built on that rule is an adaptation, not a quotation. (2) The homepage quote verifies verbatim (Diátaxis "solves problems related to documentation content (what to write), style (how to write it) and architecture (how to organise it)") but is a claim about the framework, which the finding recasts as "the type determines all three" — mild interpolation. Everything else confirmed: four types on the homepage (tutorials, how-to guides, technical reference, explanation); the two axes with the exact quote on /foundations/ ("A skill or craft or practice contains both action (practical knowledge, knowing how, what we do) and cognition (theoretical knowledge, knowing that, what we think)") plus at-work/at-study acquisition-vs-application; colophon credits "Diátaxis is the work of Daniele Procida", confirms the Divio 2014-2021 origin and the CITATION.cff file; the homepage indeed carries no author credit, matching the finding's own verification caution. The "hundreds of documentation projects" adoption claim in the tradition field was not specifically confirmed in my fetches (minor, uncited in the citation itself).

checks.name: arc42
checks.corrections: Fully confirmed at arc42.org/overview: "Created by Peter Hruschka & Gernot Starke"; all 12 sections match the finding's list exactly and in order; "Open source and free, also for commercial use"; tailorable with the one-page arc42 canvas variant ("An arc42 canvas captures a whole system on a single page"); "Proven in practice since 2005"; and "arc42 answers two questions in a pragmatic way: what should you document and communicate about your architecture, and how." The three-part grouping exists on the page with near-identical names: "Requirements & quality", "Structures & views", "Concepts, technologies, decisions" (finding renders the third as "Concepts, Technologies & Decisions" — trivial punctuation difference only).

checks.name: Docs as code
checks.corrections: Fully confirmed at writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/: exact quotes "you should be writing documentation with the same tools as code" and "a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation"; the practice list matches (Plain Text Markup — Markdown, reStructuredText, Asciidoc; Version Control — Git; Issue Trackers; Code Reviews; Automated Tests); all three books are referenced on the page (Anne Gentle's Docs Like Code, Andrew Etter's Modern Technical Writing, Diana Lakatos' Crafting Docs for Success); and the company roster is supported — the page names Google (Riona MacNamara's 2015 talk), Microsoft, Twitter, Rackspace, and AWS (plus Capital One, which the finding omits harmlessly). The finding's stated caution about making no edition/year claims for the books holds up.

input.overall_notes: Method: fetched every cited primary URL directly, plus the supporting spec/site pages each finding leans on (DITA ditamaps.html, DITA Technical Content document-types page, diataxis.fr /foundations/, /map/, /start-here/, /colophon/, arc42.org/overview), and ran targeted searches for the DITA terminology definitions, Errata 02 approval (29 June 2018), the troubleshooting topic's 1.3 debut, and glossentry's pre-1.3 history. All five sources exist at their cited URLs; no fabricated sources found. Four findings are accurately described (Diátaxis with two flagged paraphrase-strength nuances around the one-type-per-document rule). The first DITA finding requires substantive corrections: glossaryEntry is not a 1.3 addition (only troubleshooting is; glossentry existed by DITA 1.1/1.2), the root-element rule omits <dita> as a third permitted root, and the citation says Part 3 while the URL is the Part 2 edition. Direct quotes across all five findings otherwise verified verbatim against the sources.
